title: Checked and unchecked exceptions
idea: A checked exception is one the compiler makes every caller catch or declare; an unchecked exception extends `RuntimeException` and needs no declaration.
points: Subclasses of `Exception` are checked, except the `RuntimeException` branch.
Use checked when the caller can recover: retry, fall back, or ask the user.
Use unchecked for broken contracts like a null argument; fix the caller instead.
Interview signal: catch the narrowest type, and never let a catch hide a bug.

hero.title: Where each exception sits in Java

steps.caption: Anything you can `throw` is a `Throwable`. Its subclasses decide what the compiler checks.
`Error` covers JVM failures such as running out of memory. Application code should let them propagate.
`Exception` and its subclasses are checked. A method that throws one must catch it or declare `throws`.
`IOException` and your own `FeedDownException` are checked: failures the caller can recover from by retrying or falling back.
`RuntimeException` is the exception to the rule. It and its subclasses are unchecked.
`IllegalArgumentException` and `NullPointerException` mean a caller broke the contract. Fix the code; do not catch them.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: `throws Exception` forces a catch-all, and the catch-all hides a missing price and a bug alike.

walk.text: `throws Exception` is the widest checked type. It tells callers nothing about what can actually fail.
A null `sku` throws `NullPointerException` here. That is a bug, not a missing price.
Forced to catch something, the caller catches everything and returns 0.
Compare the coffee and null lines: a missing price and a bug are now indistinguishable.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: A specific checked exception for a recoverable outage; an unchecked one for the bug.

walk.text: `FeedDownException` extends `Exception`, so it is checked. An outage is temporary and recoverable.
`price` declares the specific type. A null `sku` fails fast with an unchecked exception.
A simple not-found is better as Optional (c05-t03); checked exceptions suit failures the caller can recover from.
`Checkout` catches only the checked type and recovers: the last known price, or a retry message.
The bug is not caught by `describe`. It travels up to a last-resort handler and gets noticed.

pitfalls: An empty `catch (Exception e)` turns bugs like a null key into silent defaults.
Declaring `throws Exception` forces every caller to catch everything; declare the specific type.
Wrapping without passing the cause loses the original stack trace; use `new X(msg, e)`.

quiz.q: What happens when you compile this method?
options: It compiles; any IOException surfaces only at runtime
It compiles with an unchecked warning
It compiles because IOException is a RuntimeException
quiz.why: `Files.writeString` declares `IOException`, which is checked. The method must catch it or add `throws IOException` to its signature.

takeaway: Checked for failures callers can handle; unchecked for bugs callers must fix.
